item.title: Asymmetric Little--Parks Oscillations as a Probe of Coupled Pairing Channels in Surface-Superconducting \texorpdfstring{PtBi$_2$}{PtBi2}
item.description: arXiv:2611.01764v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Motivated by the recent discovery of unconventional surface superconductivity in PtBi$_{2}$, we theoretically study its signatures in the Little-Parks oscillations of a narrow ring made from the same material. Using a Ginzburg-Landau model with three coupled pairing channels allowed by the trigonal crystal symmetry, we show that a fixed in-plane magnetic field can make the mean-field transition temperature asymmetric under reversal of the normal flux through the ring, while preserving periodicity in the superconducting flux quantum. The leading weak-field contribution to this asymmetry is cubic in the in-plane field strength. The flux-odd component respects the threefold crystal symmetry and changes sign when the in-plane field is rotated by $\pi/3$ at fixed magnitude. Within the homogeneous ring model, this asymmetry is absent for a single pairing channel and arises from the coupling between the three channels. Our calculations further show that increasing the in-plane magnetic field can enhance the superconducting nucleation temperature through mixing of pairing channels, illustrating magnetic control of multicomponent superconductivity in mesoscopic rings. Little-Parks interferometry with independent control of flux and field direction thus offers a mesoscopic probe of the pairing state, complementary to spectroscopic studies of the gap structure.
item.dc:creator: Yuriy Yerin, Stefan-Ludwig Drechsler, Carsten Timm, Jeroen van den Brink

item.title: Pore-scale mechanisms of capillary imbibition in cement-based materials revealed by direct numerical simulations in a realistic FIB-SEM microstructure
item.description: arXiv:2611.01901v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Moisture transport in cement-based materials involves transient multiphase flow through highly irregular pore networks, where evolving air--water interfaces strongly influence liquid invasion and gas displacement. Here, pore-resolved, image-based direct numerical simulations (DNS) are used to investigate spontaneous imbibition in a FIB--SEM-reconstructed cementitious microstructure, resolving air--water interface dynamics at nanometre-to-micrometre spatial scales and nanosecond-to-microsecond timescales. As these dynamics remain inaccessible to direct experimental observation at such scales, the simulations provide, to the best of our knowledge, the first direct view of transient imbibition within the capillary porosity of a realistic cementitious microstructure. The three-dimensional simulations reveal highly heterogeneous wetting-front propagation, continuous interface reconfiguration, and progressive air entrapment, showing that local dynamics depend on evolving interface curvature and capillary-pressure fields rather than on characteristic pore size alone. Significant air entrapment develops even within the capillary pores and under perfectly water-wetting conditions, progressively reducing the saturation rate, while the capillary pressure of trapped-air clusters depends strongly on local interface geometry rather than gas volume alone. Controlled two-dimensional analyses show that the balance between capillary, viscous, inertial, and gravitational effects is strongly scale-dependent. Comparison with the three-dimensional simulations highlights the importance of out-of-plane interface curvature and pore-network connectivity. The framework also resolves moisture conditions at the steel--concrete interface, illustrating its potential for corrosion-relevant pore-scale analysis.
item.dc:creator: Luka Malenica, Zhidong Zhang, Ueli Angst

item.title: Controlling the Sign and Magnitude of the Thermoreflectance Coefficient of Gold-MoS$_2$ Metamaterials
item.description: arXiv:2611.02024v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Heating a material changes how much light it reflects. This effect, quantified by the thermoreflectance coefficient $C_\mathrm{TR}$, enables temperature sensing, while it is a nuisance for situations where constant reflection is crucial. Whereas temperature detection requires a large $C_\mathrm{TR}$, the latter situation demands it to be as close to zero as possible. Controlling the $C_\mathrm{TR}$ has so far relied on the selection of materials and wavelengths, rather than engineering the coefficient itself. This work demonstrates that the $C_\mathrm{TR}$ of a 50 nm thin gold film on SiO$_2$/Si can be controlled in sign and magnitude by an ultrathin ($<$8 nm) MoS$_2$ film underneath it. Time-resolved thermoreflectance measurements reveal suppression, sign inversion, and revival of the thermoreflectance signal, controlled by three knobs: ($i$) the buried MoS$_2$ thickness, ($ii$) probe wavelength, and ($iii$) ambient temperature. Transfer-matrix simulations using temperature-dependent dielectric functions of gold and MoS$_2$ reproduce all experimental observations, demonstrating an optothermal metamaterial platform with controllable properties. In particular, these (anti-)thermoreflective metamaterial mirrors bring $C_\mathrm{TR}$ under the same interference design rules previously applied to the optical response itself, opening ways to maximize or minimize the temperature dependence of the optical reflectance, tailored to the specific application.
item.dc:creator: D. Saleta Reig, B. Liu, K. Xu, J. S. Reparaz, K. -J. Tielrooij

item.title: Magnetically and electrically tunable nonlinear Hall effect in Tt-symmetric antiferromagnets
item.description: arXiv:2611.02567v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Tt-symmetric antiferromagnets can exhibit multiferroicity with coexisting ferroelectricity and magnetic order, and thus host multiple order-parameter configurations. However, how to electrically read out these configurations is an issue meriting further investigation. Here, by combining tight-binding and first-principles calculations, we propose electrically and magnetically tunable nonlinear Hall transport in ferroelectric Tt-symmetric antiferromagnets. Model calculations show that ferroelectric switching can reverse the sign of the Berry curvature dipole (BCD), whereas the Neel vector rotation modulates its magnitude, allowing both ferroelectric and magnetic order to be reflected in the nonlinear Hall signal. First-principles calculations of the VOCl2 monolayer confirm these behaviors and predict a sizable BCD that gives rise to a potentially detectable Hall voltage. Our findings open up opportunities to integrate electrical and magnetic modulations of the nonlinear Hall effect within a single material, with potential applications in multi-state information encoding and readout in antiferromagnetic spintronics.
item.dc:creator: Yueyue Ning, Yongliang Song, Yanrui Ding, Zhichao Zhou, Xiao Li

item.title: Organizational Learning in Materials Discovery Campaigns: Which Databases, Calculations, and Agent Teams Pay Off
item.description: arXiv:2611.02571v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: More databases can make a materials campaign worse. Through an organizational lens, we trace each source's contribution. One band-gap campaign ranks seven anion families from archived measured gaps, one vote per source. In the first half of its budget, all seven pooled rank worse (rank agreement 0.737; 1 = measured order) than the best pool of three (0.851). As a stability check, choosing the pool on half the runs and testing on the rest kept the gap. Splitting Materials Project afterwards points to its transition-metal oxides and fluorides. Two databases from one pipeline add nothing over one, but pooling gives their shared ordering two votes. New calculations repay their cost early only when two or three campaigns reuse them. Flat language-model agent teams trailed a random-pick baseline (mean 0.876, sd 0.096, 20 searches). An adaptive Al-Mg-Si team, mostly interatomic potentials, was scored on unseen HSE06 calculations. In its first quarter of compute it found 49% of the ten lowest-formation-energy compounds, against at most 40% for fixed teams and 73% for MACE-MP-0 alone. Merging members whose orderings agreed carried most of its gain. This suggests pooling a few sources that fit the measurements, counting each pipeline once and charging for computation.
item.dc:creator: Kinston Ack\"olf, Taylor D. Sparks

item.title: Derivation of Novel Isotropic Metamaterials at the Hashin Shtrikman Stiffness Limit Enabled by Physics Informed Neural Networks
item.description: arXiv:2611.02622v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Current methods of deriving ultrastiff isotropic metamaterials require heuristics or topology optimization, which are highly inefficient and limited by human input. To circumvent this, Physics Informed Neural Networks are applied to analytical equations to systematically solve for plate orientations in closed cell lattices. Following a standardized procedure, the plate orientations were modelled and assembled into geometries resembling quasi random foams for validation via finite element simulations. Closed cell 6-plate geometries were also additively manufactured using LAPIS and experimentally characterized. The results indicate that a minimum of 6 plates is required to constitute an ultrastiff isotropic lattice, 7 plates would return the established plate Cubic Octet structure while 8 to 10 plate geometries did not show significant differences in properties. Despite the introduction of some plate bending due to sub-optimal plate placement strategy, relative stiffness of the PINNs lattices adheres closely to the Hashin Shtrikman upper bound, 90 percent of Hashin Shtrikman upper bound at a relative density of 0.4, and the lattices maintain near isotropic behaviour, achieving a Zener ratio of 0.95 at a relative density of 0.1. Benchmarking results show that specific stiffness of PINNs lattices is higher than the majority of isotropic architectures reported in the literature.
item.dc:creator: Manish Kumar Singh, Dominic Kang Jueh Lim, Anson Wen Han Cheong, Adams Wai Kin Kong, Chang Quan Lai

item.title: Observing oscillations using the non-magnetic and magnetic spin Hall effect in a non-collinear antiferromagnet
item.description: arXiv:2611.02804v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In this study, it was observed that, in non-collinear IrMn3, both the non-magnetic spin Hall effect (NMSHE) and the magnetic spin Hall effect (MSHE) exhibit oscillations as the triangularly ordered magnetic moments of IrMn3 evolve with temperature. These oscillations are strongly influenced by the magnetic properties at the interface between IrMn3 and the adjacent material. Permalloy (Py), a ferromagnet, and platinum (Pt), a paramagnet, were employed as adjacent layers. Such experimental analyses demonstrate the pioneering nature of this phenomenon, which is validated through magnetoresistance measurements performed under different experimental conditions.
item.dc:creator: Monalisa Cavalcante, Jos\'e Laurentino, Carlos Eduardo, Kevin Mesel, Jos\'e Holanda

item.title: Superinsulation, electric confinement in condensed matter
item.description: arXiv:2611.02841v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Superinsulation is the confining phase of condensed matter systems. It is a genuine quantum state of matter, dual to superconductivity, just as confinement in particle physics is dual to the Higgs phase. In contrast to hadron physics, the gauge field that becomes confining is not colour SU(3) but the conventional U(1) electromagnetic field. Superinsulation arises in superconductors with an emergent granular condensate when core-less XY vortices between condensate grains become tensionless, unobservable Dirac strings and magnetic monopoles are liberated and condense. This magnetic condensate confines electric fields into flux tubes, strings that generate a linear potential between Cooper pairs. These dual Abrikosov flux tubes give rise to infinite electrical resistance, persisting up to a finite deconfinement temperature. We shall review the theoretical framework of superinsulation together with its experimental validation, including the direct observation of the linear confining potential and we shall stress how phase-only approaches and disorder-based ideas for the phases around the superconductor-to-insulator transition are hard to reconcile with recent experimental observations.
item.dc:creator: M. Cristina Diamantini, Carlo A. Trugenberger

item.title: Site-orbit masked twin-branch Transformer for symmetry-constrained crystal generation
item.description: arXiv:2611.02906v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Generative models for crystal structure prediction (CSP) have expanded the search space for novel materials and improved screening efficiency. However, simultaneously generating stable and novel structures remains challenging because of the complex structural and physical constraints governing crystals. To address this challenge, we propose site-orbit masked twin-branch Transformer model (ST2M), a symmetry-guided discrete--continuous diffusion framework incorporating degree-of-freedom masks and conditioned on Wyckoff patterns. ST2M represents crystal structures as sequences of independent occupied Wyckoff orbits and employs a twin-branch Transformer to jointly denoise discrete and continuous variables. In our experiments, ST2M achieves a structural validity of 96.37\%. For known patterns in dataset, 23.86\% of generated structures simultaneously satisfy stability, uniqueness, and novelty criteria, representing a relative improvement of 68.15\% over the best-performing baseline. First-principles calculations identify a total of 21 previously unreported stable structures among selected candidates with low predicted energies. These results demonstrate that ST2M can generate chemically viable crystal candidates under prescribed crystallographic constraints and generalize to unknown Wyckoff patterns, providing a practical route to accelerated materials discovery.
item.dc:creator: Junchi Liu, Haoran Si, Luo Yan, Sergei Tretiak, Liujiang Zhou

item.title: A combined segmented anode gas ionization chamber and time-of-flight detector for heavy ion elastic recoil detection analysis
item.description: arXiv:2611.03147v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A dedicated detector system for heavy ion elastic recoil detection analysis at the Tandem Laboratory of Uppsala University is presented. Benefits of combining a time-of-flight measurement with a segmented anode gas ionization chamber are demonstrated. The capability of ion species identification is improved with the present system, compared to that obtained when using a single solid state silicon detector for the full ion energy signal. The system enables separation of light elements, up to Neon, based on atomic number while signals from heavy elements such as molybdenum and tungsten are separated based on mass, to a sample depth on the order of one micrometer. The performance of the system is discussed and a selection of material analysis applications is given. Plasma-facing materials from fusion experiments, in particular metal mirrors, are used as a main example for the discussion. Marker experiments using nitrogen-15 or oxygen-18 are specific cases for which the described improved species separation and sensitivity are required. Resilience to radiation damage and significantly improved energy resolution for heavy elements at low energies are additional benefits of the gas ionization chamber over a solid state detector based system.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: P. Str\"om, P. Petersson, M. Rubel, G. Possnert, Review of Scientific Instruments 87 (10), 103303, 2016
item.dc:creator: Petter Str\"om, Per Petersson, Marek Rubel, G\"oran Possnert

item.title: PaddleMaterials: An End-to-End Deep Learning Toolkit for Materials Science
item.description: arXiv:2611.03154v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Machine learning supports materials design, atomistic simulation and experimental characterization, yet models and workflows remain fragmented. We present PaddleMaterials, an open-source framework integrating heterogeneous materials-learning tasks while preserving task-specific representations and scientific semantics. It unifies data processing, training, evaluation, pretrained-model management and workflows across six task classes: property prediction, structure generation, machine-learning interatomic potentials, electronic-structure fields, spectrum elucidation and microscopy image processing. Task interfaces record physical quantities, units, aggregation conventions and references, making cross-task composition verifiable. A shared compiler backend enables switching from dynamic-graph to compiled execution through one setting, using graph optimization, operator fusion and hardware-targeted code generation without changing model definitions. Across 65 model instances in 11 groups, compiled execution accelerated every instance in eight groups, with group median speedups of 11%-224% and group maximum speedups of 11%-336%. Case studies on LiMnO2 and toluene link structure generation or spectrum elucidation, interatomic-potential relaxation, property prediction and electron-density prediction, using same-geometry density functional theory (DFT) calculations as references. For LiMnO2, predicted formation energies for generated and relaxed structures differed from same-geometry PBE+U references by at most 7 meV per atom, while the computational cost of model steps was less than one-twentieth of a DFT single-point calculation. PaddleMaterials extends unified materials workflows beyond conventional property, potential and structure-generation tasks while supporting verifiable cross-task operations and compiled execution.
item.dc:creator: Xuwei Liu, Zhimin Zhang, Xiaoguang Hu, Zhongwei Liu, Yuanhui Sun, Jun Huo, Hua Wu, Haifeng Wang

item.title: Identifying the Shear Piezoelectric Coefficient using Physics-Informed Neural Networks under Exact Boundary and Initial Constraints
item.description: arXiv:2611.03485v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The shear piezoelectric coefficient $e_{15}$ governs the shear-mode electromechanical coupling in piezoelectric micromachined ultrasonic transducers (PMUTs) and surface acoustic wave (SAW) devices, but measuring it typically requires destructive resonance testing on dedicated specimens. On simulated data, $e_{15}$ can instead be recovered non-destructively from sparse, noisy subsurface wavefield observations using a constrained physics-informed neural network (PINN). By building exact spatial distance functions and temporal multipliers directly into the network output, the clamped, grounded boundaries and resting initial state hold automatically, leaving the loss with only the interior equations of coupled electro-elastodynamics and the data misfit. Non-dimensional scaling brings all governing coefficients within one decade of O(1), and the setup removes the boundary and initial-condition penalty weights that soft-constraint methods must tune. In a six-way comparison (plane-strain PZT-5H, manufactured wavefield, 30 dB noise), a soft-penalty baseline with adaptive weights converges to an erroneous $e_{15}$ in four of the five runs (51.7% mean error), and fixed penalties reach an error of 0.85% only after a second-order optimization stage. The constrained formulations reach mean $e_{15}$ errors between 0.15% and 0.51% with held-out displacement errors below 1%. Within these variants, the spatial multiplier gives rapid first-order convergence, and the quadratic temporal multiplier lowers the early-time electrostatic residual by a factor of 6.8 versus a linear one. On finite-element data along one subsurface line, the full formulation recovers $e_{15}$ with 1.19% mean error at 30 dB and keeps it between 0.65% and 2.71% across a 40 to 0 dB noise sweep. Finally, training on displacements alone still recovers $e_{15}$ with mean errors of 0.45% on finite-element and 1.64% on manufactured data.
item.dc:creator: Suhas Suresh Bharadwaj

item.title: Unified Learning of Interatomic Potentials and Electronic Hamiltonians, with Applications in 2D Materials
item.description: arXiv:2510.16605v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We introduce UnIPH, an equivariant graph neural network designed to jointly predict both interatomic potentials and tight-binding (TB) Hamiltonians for an atomic structure. UnIPH is trained using density functional theory (DFT) calculations followed by Wannier projection to predict energies and forces as node-level targets and Wannier-projected TB Hamiltonians as edge-level targets. This enables physically consistent modeling of coupled mechanical-electronic responses with near-DFT-level accuracy. After separately training two UnIPH models on DFT data for bilayer graphene and monolayer MoS2, respectively, we find that these models capture key deformation-electronic effects: in twisted bilayer graphene, the trained UnIPH reveals how interlayer spacing, in-plane strain, and out-of-plane corrugation drive isolated flat-band formation, and further shows that modulating substrate interaction strength can generate flat bands even away from the magic angle (approximately 1.1 degrees). For monolayer MoS2, UnIPH accurately reproduces phonon dispersions and strain-dependent band-gap evolution, and further predicts how a non-uniform substrate creates localized strain pockets that spatially modulate the conduction- and valence-band edges.
item.dc:creator: Moon-ki Choi, Daniel Palmer, Shivam Sharma, Harley T. Johnson

item.title: INTERFACE Force Field for Alumina with Validated Bulk Phases and a pH-Resolved Surface Model Database for Aqueous, Electrolyte, and Molecular Interfaces
item.description: arXiv:2601.12570v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Alumina and aluminum oxyhydroxides underpin numerous chemical engineering technologies in heterogeneous catalysis, corrosion protection, functional coatings, energy storage devices, and biomedical components. Yet molecular models that predictively connect phase structure, pH dependent surface chemistry, electrolyte organization, and adsorption across operating conditions remain limited. Here we introduce the INTERFACE Force Field (IFF) together with a curated, ready-to-use pH-resolved surface model database for an accurate and transferable atomistic description of major alumina phases according to experimental benchmarks available. The framework covers alpha-Al2O3, gamma-Al2O3, boehmite, diaspore, and gibbsite using a single parameter set compatible with CHARMM, AMBER, OPLS-AA, CVFF, and PCFF. Simulations reproduce experimental reference data across structural, thermodynamic, mechanical, and interfacial benchmarks with deviations of few percent relative to experiment, exceeding existing force fields and density-functional approaches. We introduce a transferable treatment of surface ionization and charge regulation across alumina phases over a broad pH range, enabling simulations of realistic solid-electrolyte interfaces without phase-specific reparameterization. Quantitative reliability is demonstrated by reproducing zeta-potential trends and pH-dependent adsorption of an organic corrosion inhibitor at alumina-water interfaces. Predicted adsorption free energies and surface contact times correlate with experiments across an order of magnitude, enabling process-relevant screening and explaining limitations of earlier adsorption models. The approach is 10,000 to 100,000 times faster than DFT-machine learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) and supports the design of alumina-containing catalysts, corrosion-resistant coatings, energy storage and biomaterials under realistic process conditions.
item.dc:creator: Cheng Zhu, Krishan Kanhaiya, Samir Darouich, Sean P. Florez, Karnajit Sen, Patrick Keil, Nawel S. Khelfallah, Eduard Schreiner, Ratan K. Mishra, Hendrik Heinz

item.title: Pathway to lowest-energy structures and stress relaxation for the surface triple junction of copper
item.description: arXiv:2603.01920v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The behavior of surface triple junctions (STJ) at emergent grain boundaries on free surfaces is critical to the microstructure evolution, and therefore to the stability of next generation interconnects. Yet, despite this significant importance, its lowest-energy structure and local stress have remained persistently unknown. Here, we fill this critical gap through high-resolution experimental mapping of the local surface deformation at STJs of a symmetrical tilt grain boundaries with [111] rotation axis and misorientation angles 13.17{\deg}, the analysis of the local core-shifted structure and stress relaxation, and ergodic searching metastable structures accordingly with the molecular-statics (MS) calculation. The computation clearly shows the zipped Y-shaped notch as the lowest-energy structures for this group of STJs, the line profile of which is consistent with the experimental observation. This energetic preference was well explained by the stress delocalization mechanism and was tested for a wide range of boundaries with even deeper core-shift depth using machine learning methods based on the data obtained from MS calculation. By revealing the elusive thermodynamics of STJs, our findings advance the research field by redefining the energetic framework for capillary driven structure evolution and providing foundation for understanding kinetically diffusive deformation and for engineering thin-film interconnects and related materials.
item.dc:creator: Ipen Demirel, Yuan Fang, Yan Liu, Haitian Shan, Xiaopu Zhang, Yuchuan Shao, Jianda Shao, John J. Boland

item.title: Rationalizing defect formation energies in metals and semiconductors with semilocal density functionals
item.description: arXiv:2604.05385v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The study of defects in materials is of utmost importance for technological applications and the design of new materials. In this work, we analyze the performance of density functional approximations on two prototypical sets of defective systems: monovacancies in eight fcc metals, and interstitials in the semiconductor Si-diamond. Specifically, we compute defect formation energies using the local density approximation, the Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof generalized gradient approximation, the meta-generalized gradient approximations (meta-GGAs) strongly constrained and appropriately normed (SCAN), its regularized version (r2SCAN), the Lebeda-Aschebrock-Kummel (LAK) meta-GGA, and the Heyd-Scuseria-Ernzerhof screened hybrid functional. For metals, the local density approximation shows better performance compared to the other approximations, whereas for silicon, the meta-generalized gradient approximation Lebeda-Aschebrock-Kummel yields outstand- ing accuracy, surpassing the hybrid functional and approaching the results of more computationally demanding Quantum Monte Carlo methods. To rationalize the different performances, we study the semilocal ingredients rs, s and {\alpha} in both the pristine and defective structures. We identify critical regions that indicate the observed trends of the defect formation energies and pave the way for improving density functional approximations.
item.dc:creator: Jorge Vega Bazantes, Timo Lebeda, Akilan Ramasamy, Kanun Pokharel, Ruiqi Zhang, John Perdew, Jianwei Sun

item.title: Spatial statistics for screening molecular structures
item.description: arXiv:2605.17147v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The dominant paradigm in computational materials discovery relies on heavily parameterized deep architectures, including message-passing graph networks and equivariant models, that require millions of DFT-labeled training structures and produce non-convex latent representations that complicate continuous optimization for inverse design. These architectures are impractical in data-scarce regimes, which is the typical case in molecular screening, and exhibit well-documented limitations in capturing chemically disordered configurations and chiral geometries. This review presents feature engineering based on spatial statistics as a physically rigorous and immediately deployable alternative. Molecular structures are encoded as voxelized scalar fields, and two-point auto- and cross-correlations are evaluated deterministically via Fast Fourier Transforms, explicitly transferring the burden of spatial pattern recognition from the learning algorithm to a closed-form, physics-informed operation. Principal component analysis of the resulting correlation maps yields low-dimensional, strictly convex representations that support lean neural networks (<100k trainable parameters) and non-parametric surrogate models, achieving sub-2% prediction error with as few as 10 training samples. Demonstrated across periodic crystals, chemically disordered high-entropy alloys, and non-periodic organic molecules, this framework enables Bayesian active learning and zero-shot extrapolation on commodity hardware, which current large-scale architectures cannot replicate at equivalent data budgets.
item.dc:creator: Pranoy Ray, Surya R. Kalidindi

item.title: First-Principles Study of Fe Adsorption and Its Effects on the Mechanical and Electrical Properties of Monolayer and Bilayer Biphenylene Networks
item.description: arXiv:2605.21918v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Biphenylene network (BPN), a two-dimensional carbon allotrope, has attracted interest for its potential applications. Here, we systematically investigate Fe adsorption on monolayer and bilayer BPN using first-principles calculations, focusing on structural stability, mechanical properties, and electronic transport. On monolayer BPN, the average Fe adsorption energy generally becomes more negative with increasing Fe coverage, accompanied by nonmonotonic variations and increasingly pronounced Fe aggregation, eventually favoring three-dimensional growth. In bilayer BPN, the interlayer four-membered ring center is the most favorable adsorption site, with a single-Fe adsorption energy of -4.3 eV. Both pristine monolayer and bilayer BPN exhibit high in-plane Young's and shear moduli. Fe adsorption induces nonmonotonic changes in the in-plane stiffness of monolayer BPN, without systematic enhancement. In contrast, interlayer Fe incorporation dramatically enhances the out-of-plane stiffness of bilayer BPN. The effective out-of-plane elastic constant C33 increases from 24.59 GPa in pristine bilayer BPN to 515.63 GPa at an Fe/C ratio of 25%. Furthermore, the transport calculations reveal pronounced in-plane conductivity anisotropy, with substantially different conductivity values normalized by the relaxation time ({\sigma}/{\tau}) along the two crystallographic directions.
item.dc:creator: Xiao-Ke Zhang, Zheng-Zhe Lin

item.title: Application and Performance Assessment of Annealing Methods for Electrostatic-Energy-Based Configuration Search in Mixed Crystals
item.description: arXiv:2605.24557v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In first-principles design of solid solutions and disordered materials, exhaustive evaluation of all possible substitutional configurations is often impractical because the number of site occupations increases exponentially. Here, we develop a framework for pre-screening mixed-crystal configurations using annealing methods, where the Ewald electrostatic energy is used as the objective function. Substitutional occupations are represented by binary variables, allowing the Ewald energy to be mapped onto an Ising-type Hamiltonian and the search for low-energy configurations to be formulated as a combinatorial optimization problem. We implement this formulation using simulated annealing (SA) and quantum annealing (QA), and benchmark their performance against exhaustive search. For the small-scale system CaYAlO$_4$, SA achieved a speed-up of about 30 times, while QA achieved a speed-up of more than 100 times; both methods identified all lowest-energy configurations. For the medium-scale system $\beta$-KSbF$_4$ and the large-scale Ba-doped SiAlON system, SA achieved speed-ups of about 200--300 times while stably identifying the lowest-energy structures. In contrast, QA showed limited speed-up for the medium-scale $\beta$-KSbF$_4$ system and missed some low-energy configurations, likely due to chain breaks. These results indicate that, among the approaches examined here, SA showed comparatively robust performance for Ewald-energy-based configuration search in mixed crystals. The proposed formulation can be implemented using publicly available libraries and provides a practical route for accelerating candidate-structure generation before first-principles calculations.
item.dc:creator: Tack Saquai, Kenta Hongo, Ryo Maezono, Tom Ichibha

item.title: Controllable Quantum Spin Hall Phases in Bi$_2$Te$_3$-Family van der Waals Heterobilayers
item.description: arXiv:2606.20541v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The tunability and control of topological edge/surface states are crucial for the development of new device applications. In this work, by combining first-principles calculations and Wannier-based tight-binding methods, we show the emergence of quantum spin Hall phases in van der Waals heterostructures formed by stacking two trivial quintuple layers from the Bi$_2$Te$_3$ family. We demonstrate the tunability of the edge states under interlayer strain and external electric field effects, suggesting the possibility of switching topological edge states on/off by external control. Additionally, the quantum spin Hall edge channels remain robust against interlayer twist, highlighting their stability against external perturbations. Our results provide a new way to create and manipulate two-dimensional topological phases in systems based on Bi$_2$Te$_3$ family, which can be valuable for practical applications, such as topological field effect transistors and spintronic devices.
item.dc:creator: Emmanuel V. C. Lopes, Pedro H. Sophia, Felipe Crasto de Lima, Adalberto Fazzio

item.title: Compatibility of Martensitic Microstructures in Polycrystals
item.description: arXiv:2607.12572v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The paper studies martensitic microstructures in polycrystals, focussing on their compatibility across grain boundaries. After a reduction to the case of a planar grain boundary, the case when the grain boundary separates two constant gradients of zero energy is considered. It is shown that for cubic-to tetragonal transformations such a configuration can occur when the relative grain rotation is not in the cubic group. Then the case when the grain boundary separates two simple laminates of zero energy is considered, it being shown using a computer-assisted symbolic calculation that in the cubic-to-tetragonal case compatibility is only possible for a closed set of measure zero in the manifold of grain boundary normals and relative grain rotations, and that a similar slightly weaker result holds for cubic-to-orthorhombic transformations. The results suggest why higher-order laminates are often observed for such transformations. The Taylor set of deformation gradients is defined and studied, this set having the property that any deformation whose gradient belongs to it corresponds to a zero-energy microstructure for the polycrystal independent of grain geometry and grain rotations. New upper bounds for the Taylor set are proved for cubic-to-tetragonal and cubic-to-orthorhombic transformations, generalizing those of Bhattacharya and Kohn using the geometrically linearized theory. We give a simple proof of a related result of Peigney characterizing the positive diagonal matrices in the quasiconvex hull of the energy wells for cubic-to-tetragonal transformations.
item.dc:creator: John M. Ball, Myrto Galanopoulou

item.title: Theory of phonon-magnon hybridization and angular momentum in CrI$_3$ and CrBr$_3$
item.description: arXiv:2607.26986v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In magnetic materials angular momentum can be mediated by different carriers, including electrons, magnons, and phonons. The magnons can interact with circularly polarized phonons which are close in energy, provided specific symmetry conditions are met. If the interaction is strong enough the phonons and magnons shift in frequency and start to mix to form hybrid magneto-elastic quasi-particles. In this paper, we develop a constrained Hamiltonian framework which incorporates hybrid stiffness matrices and Berry curvatures. We quantify the degree of hybridization between phonons and magnons (up to 8% in CrI$_3$ and 25% in CrBr$_3$) using a decomposition of the total energy, which is a generalization of the norm decomposition for atomic contributions to phonons used in the literature. We also explore how the total angular momentum is conserved but shared between the phononic and magnonic subsystems upon hybridization.
item.dc:creator: Maxime Mignolet, Miquel Royo, Massimiliano Stengel, Matthieu J. Verstraete

item.title: Automated Analysis to Reveal Grain Boundary Phase Microstructures
item.description: arXiv:2608.21540v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We develop a method for analyzing grain boundary (GB) microstructures that identifies distinct interfacial phases and the dislocation line defects separating them. Similar to bulk materials, GBs can adopt multiple distinct interfacial phases and undergo first-order phase transitions. When these phases coexist, their spatial arrangement and phase junctions constitute a GB microstructure, characterized by variations in excess properties and line defects with associated dislocation content. Despite this intrinsic heterogeneity, our ability to quantitatively characterize GB microstructures remains limited, as it requires identification of individual GB phases, phase-resolved excess properties, and the Burgers content of phase junctions, capabilities not available in existing automated methods. Here, we present an automated tool that performs interfacial microstructure mapping for planar coincidence site lattice GBs. The method identifies the spatial distribution of GB phases, quantifies phase-specific excess properties, and estimates the Burgers content of GB phase junctions. We demonstrate the approach using three representative cases: (i) quantification of mass transport during diffusion-limited GB phase transformations; (ii) identification of structurally indistinguishable phases formed by vacancy and interstitial loops; and (iii) characterization of GB microstructures containing phase nuclei. More broadly, this framework enables quantitative studies of GB evolution processes, including spinodal decomposition and coarsening with direct implications for GB deformation, creep, and migration.
item.dc:creator: R. Daniel Moore, Ian S. Winter, Robert E. Rudd, Fadi Abdeljawad, Timofey Frolov

item.title: Hierarchical Fourier Phase Projection for Local Electronic Observables
item.description: arXiv:2609.37814v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We develop hierarchical Fourier phase projection (HPP) to evaluate electronic observables without explicitly constructing occupied eigenstates. Nested Fourier probes progressively cancel nearby cross terms, while exponential or algebraic density-matrix decay suppresses distant contributions. Refinement reuses all previous matrix-function responses to evaluate diverse electronic observables. Electron density and nonlocal forces illustrate diagonal extraction and off-diagonal contraction, respectively. A locality-based decay model fitted to changes across completed levels estimates residual errors from the unresolved pairs without additional matrix-function applications. Tests using fixed Kohn-Sham Hamiltonians for semiconductors, metals, and thermally perturbed silica cover different decay ranges and periodic cell geometries. About 90% of the assessed density and nonlocal force predictions lie within a factor of two of the reference errors. The probing requirements for a prescribed local accuracy show weak size dependence. This work thus provides a scalable framework linking electronic locality, observable accuracy, and computational effort in large-scale electronic-structure calculations.
item.dc:creator: Tao Hu, Weiqing Zhou, Zhichang Fu, Yechen Chen, Shengjun Yuan

item.title: Trust-Limited Machine-Learning-Accelerated Nudged Elastic Band Calculations for Small-Polaron Hopping in Rutile TiO2
item.description: arXiv:2610.16850v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Nudged elastic band (NEB) calculations of small-polaron hopping are demanding because nuclear motion is coupled to a self-consistent localized electronic state. Near the charge-transfer region, slow self-consistent-field convergence, localization switching, and competing electronic solutions complicate surrogate-assisted optimization. We develop a Gaussian-process-assisted NEB workflow for this regime and demonstrate electron small-polaron hopping in rutile TiO2 using spin-polarized density functional theory with a Hubbard U correction (DFT+U ) with SIESTA. A joint energy-force Gaussian process (GP) with a Mat\'ern covariance model advances the elastic band, while active-atom root-mean-square and maximum-atom displacement limits constrain surrogate motion relative to evaluated configurations. Reaching these limits triggers first-principles sampling without requiring full surrogate convergence. Three independently DFT-verified 96-atom [001] calculations using 11, 13, and 15 images and different surrogate settings and GP parameterizations yield barriers of 0.1645, 0.1637, and 0.1640 eV, respectively, spanning 0.793 meV. In the 15-image calculation, repeated central-image sampling activates a separately calibrated local GP during surrogate optimization. Final full-band DFT verification gives a maximum projected NEB force of 0.0346 eV/{\AA}. A 324-atom calculation yields a lower barrier of 0.1302 eV, indicating supercell sensitivity and demonstrating feasibility at larger GP observation dimension. The workflow combines controlled surrogate extrapolation, targeted charge-transfer-region interpolation, and independent DFT verification to obtain polaron migration pathways, emphasizing reproducible barriers and full-band force convergence.
item.dc:creator: Ashish Kumar Singh, Irina V. Lebedeva

item.title: Structural characterization of the rutile-GeO2/TiO2 (001) heterointerface
item.description: arXiv:2610.31934v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Rutile-GeO2 (r-GeO2) has emerged as a promising ultrawide-bandgap (UWBG) semiconductor for future high-power device applications because of its favorable combination of physical and electrical properties. This study has used high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HR-TEM) to compare heterointerfaces between thin films of GeO2 grown by metal-organic chemical vapor deposition on closely-lattice-matched rutile TiO2 (r-TiO2) substrates at temperatures of 840{\deg} C and 925{\deg} C. Cross-sectional TEM observations reveal interfaces with two entirely different structures: an amorphous GeOx/r-TiO2 heterostructure with an abrupt, highly faceted and non-planar interface, or a fully epitaxial r-GeO2/r-TiO2 heterostructure characterized by a more wavy but often facetted interface. Structural analysis of the latter sample revealed a high density of strain-relieving interfacial dislocations, identified primarily as Lomer-type or 60{\deg}-type, that accommodated the ~4% lattice mismatch between the two materials, while chemical analysis showed very limited interfacial intermixing. Crystallographic analysis showed that the interface faceting was associated with rutile {101} facets, with characteristic facet angles of ~114{\deg}; these observations support thermally driven TiO2 (001) substrate faceting rather than an interface reconstruction resulting from GeO2 epitaxy. Overall, these findings provide useful insights into the mechanisms governing interface formation and strain relaxation in r-GeO2/r-TiO2 heterostructures and suggest that further refinement of growth conditions should enable improved epitaxial growth of r-GeO2 for future ultrawide-bandgap electronic device applications.
item.dc:creator: Imteaz Rahaman, Martha R. McCartney, David J. Smith, Kai Fu

item.title: Temperature-dependent magnetic properties of the antiferromagnet Mn$_2$Au
item.description: arXiv:2610.35153v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Mn$_2$Au is one of the most promising materials for antiferromagnetic spintronics due to its high N\'eel temperature, moderate anisotropy, layered spin structure allowing current induced spin-orbit-torques, and ultrafast spin dynamics. Further understanding and control of the magnetic order in Mn$_2$Au for ultrafast spintronics applications via ultrashort electric/optical means requires accurate understanding of how its magnetic properties depend on temperature. Here we present atomistic spin dynamics simulations of the temperature-dependent macroscopic magnetic properties of Mn$_2$Au single crystals. We introduce a spin Hamiltonian based on previous ab initio calculations which produces temperature-dependent scaling of the anisotropy constants with magnetisation consistent with Zener-Akulov-Callen-Callen power laws. The calculated temperature dependence of exchange stiffness follows a scaling law with magnetisation of $m^{1.83}_e$ , and predicts a temperature-dependent domain wall width that agrees very well with direct simulation. Our model provides an understanding of temperature-dependent magnetic properties of Mn$_2$Au that enables large-scale simulation of the working conditions of spintronic devices.
item.dc:creator: Jackson L. Ross, Sarah Jenkins, Ricardo Rama-Eiroa, Paul-Iulian Gavriloaea, Jack Collings, Unai Atxitia, Oksana Chubykalo-Fesenko, Karin Everschor-Sitte, Rub\'en M. Otxoa, Roy W. Chantrell, Richard F. L. Evans

item.title: Theory of Berry Singularity Markers: Diagnosing Topological Phase Transitions via Lock-In Tomography
item.description: arXiv:2111.12957v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This work brings forward an alternative approach for inferring the topological character of phase transitions in insulators. The method relies on subjecting the system of interest to a set of external fields which consist of two parts, i.e., a weak spatiotemporally slowly-varying component on top of a constant offset. This process maps the Berry singularities dictating the bulk band structure of the insulator to a synthetic space spanned by the control parameters of the external fields. By measuring the response of the system to the weak part of the perturbations, when these are additionally chosen to form spacetime textures, one can construct a quantity that is here-termed Berry singularity marker (BSM). The BSM enables the Berry singularity detection as it becomes nonzero only in the close vicinity of a Berry singularity and is equal to its charge. Moreover, near the Berry singularities, the BSM encodes the quantum metric tensor of the system. An advantage of the present method is that it can be implemented in a lock-in fashion, thus allowing to ``filter out'' disorder effects, therefore opening the door to the resilient diagnosis of topological phase transitions.
item.dc:creator: Panagiotis Kotetes

item.title: Coexistence of broadband conduction and amplitude-driven topological confinement in synthetic acoustic matter
item.description: arXiv:2408.16801v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Nonlinear and topological wave phenomena offer new opportunities for robust wave manipulation. Existing experimental platforms have largely focused on on-site (Kerr-like) nonlinearities within tight-binding frameworks, leaving the regime of programmable nonlinear inter-site coupling in far-field scattering systems essentially unexplored. Here we demonstrate a programmable acoustic metamaterial that exhibits amplitude-driven topological confinement of sound while simultaneously maintaining broadband linear transmission across the same frequency range. The system consists of an open acoustic waveguide coupled to a chain of actively controlled electroacoustic resonators enabling tunable nonlinear and nonlocal interactions. Using a classical wave-scattering model we show that increasing the excitation amplitude drives a robust topological interface mode localized deep within the structure, with the confinement strengthening continuously with drive rather than at a finite threshold. The predictions are verified experimentally using a fully programmable metacrystal composed of individually controlled acoustic resonators, enabling real-time manipulation of coupling parameters. The mode's topological origin is established by symmetry: it survives coupling disorder beyond 50% of nominal but collapses when a delay between adjacent couplings is introduced, effectively breaking the protecting chiral symmetry. These results establish a versatile platform for studying nonlinear topological wave physics and for designing adaptive acoustic metamaterials.
item.dc:creator: Mathieu Padlewski, Maxime Volery, Romain Fleury, Herv\'e Lissek, Xinxin Guo

item.title: Continuous SUN (Stable, Unique, and Novel) Metric for Generative Modeling of Inorganic Crystals
item.description: arXiv:2510.12405v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: To address pressing scientific challenges such as climate change, increasingly sophisticated generative models are being developed to efficiently sample the large chemical space of potential functional materials. The proliferation of these models has necessitated the establishment of rigorous evaluation metrics. While uniqueness (U), novelty (N), and stability (S) of samples serve as standard metrics, their current formulations show several limitations. U and N rely on binary comparisons of crystals, rendering them dependent on heuristic thresholds, incapable of quantifying the degree of similarity, sensitive to atomic coordinate perturbations, and not invariant to sample permutation. Similarly, the binary assessment of S risks a premature exclusion of marginally unstable yet potentially novel candidates. These limitations are addressed by making the aforementioned metrics continuous. Furthermore, we integrate them into a unified metric ``continuous SUN" (cSUN), which offers a smoother score distribution and greater tunability than the conventional binary SUN metric. Experimental results demonstrate that our continuous metrics provide granular insights into sample distributions and secondarily serve as a soft screening score for selecting samples for further analysis. Finally, the use of cSUN as a reward signal in reinforcement learning is explored, showing that its adjustable weighting scheme effectively enhances sample diversity and convergence to a better optima in a Chemeleon2 case study.
item.dc:creator: Masahiro Negishi, Hyunsoo Park, Kinga O. Mastej, Aron Walsh

item.title: Unlocking n-alk-1-ynes Conformers: Quantum "Trigger Finger" versus "Stiff Joint" Conformations
item.description: arXiv:2511.02470v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Molecular conformation in n-alk-1-ynes (CnA) is conventionally simplified to an all-planar structure. We report a comprehensive quantum chemical analysis revealing two near-isoenergetic rotamers at the acetylenic terminus: planar (C$_s$) and skewed (C$_1$). The high, symmetric rotational energy barrier ($\approx 150$\,meV) arises from unique steric relief near the $\mathrm{sp}$ center coupled with electronic stabilization of C$_1$. This creates a unique kinetic profile: a Quantum ``Trigger Finger'' ($\alpha$ rotation) that enforces an $\approx 50\%:\,50\%$ $\mathrm{C}_s/\mathrm{C}_1$ ensemble, sharply contrasting with the thermodynamically biased ``Stiff Joint'' ($\delta$ rotation) of the alkyl chain. This structural degeneracy necessitates ensemble averaging for spectroscopic data interpretation, while the slow interconversion permits kinetic trapping and intentional conformer enrichment during synthesis and molecular junction fabrication. Our work redefines the alkyne anchor, providing a blueprint for accurate interpretation of spectroscopic data and achieving conformational control in molecular electronics.
item.dc:creator: Ioan B\^aldea

item.title: Thermomagnonic Torques in Insulating Altermagnets
item.description: arXiv:2512.14660v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We develop a symmetry-controlled theory of anisotropic thermomagnonic torques in insulating altermagnets. Starting from the stochastic LLG equations, we identify a spin-splitter magnonic torque associated with thermally generated, sublattice-odd spin currents and an anisotropic entropic torque dictated by crystal symmetry. These torques produce anisotropic magnetic-texture responses to temperature gradients. In particular, thermally generated spin currents induce domain-wall precession, which reduces domain-wall velocities for selected gradient directions. We also predict an anisotropic skyrmion Hall response, with symmetry-selected directions enabling fast skyrmion motion with strongly suppressed transverse deflection. Our results reveal experimentally testable symmetry fingerprints of insulating altermagnets and extend more broadly to anisotropic magnets with exchange-driven magnon spin splitting.
item.dc:creator: Edward Schwartz, Hamed Vakili, Alexey A. Kovalev

item.title: MSP-LLM: A Structured Large Language Model Framework for Inorganic Material Synthesis Planning
item.description: arXiv:2602.07543v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Material synthesis planning (MSP) remains a fundamental and underexplored bottleneck in AI-driven materials discovery, as it requires not only identifying suitable precursor materials but also designing coherent sequences of synthesis operations to realize a target material. Although several AI-based approaches have been proposed to address isolated subtasks of MSP, a methodology for solving the entire MSP task has yet to be established. We propose MSP-LLM, a structured LLM-based framework that formulates MSP as a two-stage process composed of two constituent subproblems: precursor prediction (PP) and synthesis operation prediction (SOP). Our approach introduces a discrete material class as an intermediate decision variable that organizes both tasks into a chemically consistent decision chain. For SOP, we further incorporate hierarchical precursor types as synthesis-relevant inductive biases and employ precursor constraint factorization that preserves precursor-related information in the autoregressive decoding state. Extensive experiments show that MSP-LLM consistently outperforms existing methods on both PP and SOP, as well as on the MSP task, demonstrating an effective and scalable framework with practical potential for autonomous MSP.
item.dc:creator: Heewoong Noh, Gyoung S. Na, Namkyeong Lee, Chanyoung Park

item.title: All-electron Dynamical Bethe-Salpeter Equation for Extended Systems with Atom-centered Orbital Basis
item.description: arXiv:2606.08350v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Solving Bethe-Salpeter equation (BSE) for the two-particle Green's function is the most widely used approach for taking into account the particle-hole (exciton) interaction in electronic excitation in the context of the many-body theory based on Green's function. In BSE calculations, the static approximation to the screened Coulomb interaction kernel is commonly employed. However, when the excitonic character is significant as typically indicated by a large exciton binding energy, dynamical screening effects become non-negligible, rendering the static approximation questionable. Because of the large computational cost due to the dense Brillouin zone integration necessary for convergence, solving the dynamical BSE for extended systems remains a significant challenge, especially when combined with GW calculation for the calculation of quasi-particle energies. In this work, we formulate the plane-wave based effective dielectric function method [Zhang, et al., Phys. Rev. B 107, 235205 (2023)] for the dynamical BSE calculation using atom-centered orbitals as basis functions. We implement this approach in our recently developed all-electron numerical atom-centered orbital (NAO) implementation of BSE@GW [Zhou, et. al. J. Chem. Theory Comput. 21, 291 (2025)] for extended systems. We validate our all-electron NAO-based implementation of the dynamical BSE method, and we then discuss its realistic application to molecular crystal of naphthalene by performing the dynamical BSE@G0W0 calculation.
item.dc:creator: Ruiyi Zhou, Songrui Liu, Jianhang Xu, Yi Yao, Yosuke Kanai

item.title: Helical Domain-Wall-Ring Networks Reshape Superconducting Correlations
item.description: arXiv:2606.23599v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Extended domain-wall networks that emerge in moir\'e materials provide a distinct platform for quasi-one-dimensional electronic states. However, the interaction-driven orders in confined networks remain largely unexplored. Here, we discuss superconducting (SC) correlations in interacting helical domain-wall-ring networks in the closed topological domains formed within the moir\'e patterns of an underlying twisted bilayer honeycomb lattice. We first analyze the system within the framework of an infinite-size theory and show that inter-ring SC-pair tunneling is renormalization-group relevant in an appropriate interaction regime, favoring enhanced SC correlations through inter-ring phase locking. To address finite-size effects resulting from the ring-network geometry, we present a self-consistent variational approach. Our analysis shows that even in the regime where the infinite-size theory predicts strongly coupled pair tunneling, the induced phase-locking scale remains strongly suppressed. In contrast, the SC scaling dimension is governed mainly by density-density interactions and ring geometry, decreasing modestly with decreasing twist angle while remaining insensitive to the pair-tunneling strength. This discrepancy demonstrates that ring networks cannot generally be understood as simple finite-size truncations of their infinite-size counterparts but can exhibit qualitatively distinct collective behavior. Our study highlights how the interplay of confinement effects and ring-network geometry can reshape SC correlations.
item.dc:creator: Yi-Chun Hung, Arun Bansil

item.title: Unconventional Mixed-Parity Magnetism in Rare-Earth Tetraborides
item.description: arXiv:2607.02117v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Altermagnetism has advanced the study of compensated magnets by revealing non-relativistic spin splitting, traditionally classified into strictly even- or odd-parity spin textures. Here, we establish component-resolved mixed-parity spin splitting in a fully three-dimensional compensated magnet and identify its microscopic origin. Using first-principles calculations, tight-binding and $\mathbf{k} \cdot \mathbf{p}$ models, along with spin-group symmetry analysis, we demonstrate that the non-coplanar ground state of $\mathrm{TbB}_4$ enforces odd-parity $p$- and $f$-wave-like textures for the in-plane spin components while the out-of-plane component retains an even-parity $d$-wave altermagnetic character. Crucially, the $p$-wave texture is driven not by relativistic spin-orbit coupling but by a staggered emergent flux arising from the scalar spin chirality of the non-coplanar order. This mixed-parity structure dictates distinct transport fingerprints, including bulk non-relativistic Edelstein and spin Hall responses that respond characteristically to reversal of the chirality domains. Spin-orbit coupling additionally enables a Berry curvature dipole. These results establish the rare-earth tetraborides as a robust platform for engineering complex spin-charge conversion phenomena.
item.dc:creator: Dong-Choon Ryu, Jae-Ho Han, Bongjae Kim, Chang-Jong Kang

item.title: Quantifying translational and bond-orientational order metrics in hyperuniform and nonhyperuniform many-particle systems
item.description: arXiv:2609.10359v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Quantifying the degree of order/disorder in many-particle systems remains an outstanding problem in physics, materials science, and mathematics. To this end, we consider the translational order metric $\tau_T$, defined as the squared $L^2$ norm of the total correlation function $h(\mathbf{r})$, and introduce its bond-orientational analogue $\tau_O$, defined from the weighted total correlation function $h_{\mathbf{f}}(\mathbf{r})$ using local orientational weights (S. Torquato et al., Phys. Rev. X 16, 011042 (2026)). The pair $(\tau_T,\tau_O)$ places both forms of order on a common two-point statistical footing. We compute both metrics for two nonhyperuniform sphere-packing models in 2D and 3D as functions of packing fraction $\phi$: 1) equilibrium hard particles and 2) nonequilibrium random sequential addition (RSA) packings. For the nonhyperuniform systems, bond-orientational order remains subdominant along the equilibrium-fluid and RSA configurations; however, its magnitude relative to the translational metric increases near the upper end of the equilibrium-fluid branches, much more strongly in 2D than in 3D, and the two metrics become comparable along the sampled crystal branches. At common packing fractions, equilibrium fluids and RSA packings trace distinct $(\tau_T,\tau_O)$ trajectories, revealing preparation-dependent differences in structural order. As a representative hyperuniform family, we study 2D disordered stealthy hyperuniform (SHU) ground states for $0<\chi<1/2$, where $\chi$ is the stealthiness parameter. Within the disordered SHU phase, bond-orientational order remains subdominant, but its magnitude relative to the translational metric increases toward the disorder-to-order threshold. In all three models, $\tau_T$ and $\tau_O$ are positively correlated beyond the Poisson-reference regime: $\tau_O$ increases monotonically with $\tau_T$ across the sampled state points.
item.dc:creator: Anirban Mukherjee, Salvatore Torquato

item.title: Spin splitting without symmetry: a nearly compensated ferrimagnet and the origin of altermagnetism
item.description: arXiv:2609.12931v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The spin splitting of collinear altermagnets is usually attributed to the crystal symmetry relating the opposite-spin sublattices --- a rotation or mirror in place of the translation or inversion of a conventional antiferromagnet. We show that this symmetry organizes the splitting but does not produce it; its origin is the anisotropic arrangement of the magnetic orbitals and their ligands, which also fixes the symmetry itself. Two results establish this. A triclinic ($P1$) \ce{Mn} oxide, a fully compensated ferrimagnet whose two inequivalent sublattices are related by no symmetry, is spin split throughout the Brillouin zone; repositioning the same ligands, atom for atom, to restore an inversion centre relating the two metal sites collapses the splitting to a residual two orders of magnitude smaller, so the splitting follows from the arrangement rather than the symmetry. Symmetry, we show formally, can only ever reverse or forbid a splitting that already exists: it cannot create one between sublattices an arrangement has left electronically identical, nor where the underlying orbitals carry no anisotropy to arrange in the first place. Organizing the analysis through an operation-resolved symmetry hierarchy and reading the crystal classes as a single axis, the enforced nodal planes fall from two to one to zero across the orthorhombic, monoclinic, and triclinic classes while the arrangement-generated splitting persists to the base. The altermagnet and the fully compensated ferrimagnet are thus the two ends of one axis --- the same splitting, organized by symmetry at one end and unorganized at the other --- and the search for compensated spin-split magnets is a search over orbital arrangements rather than symmetry labels.
item.dc:creator: Jaekyung Jang, Joo Yull Rhee

item.title: Time-temperature-composition equivalence of the glass transition in digitally mixed 3D-printed polymers
item.description: arXiv:2610.14986v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: For more than seventy years, time-temperature equivalence (TTE) has enabled a few measurements to describe the linear viscoelasticity of polymers over many decades of frequency. Multimaterial 3D printing now combines elastomeric and glassy resins voxel by voxel into digitally mixed polymers. Composition shifts the glass transition along the frequency axis, as temperature does, but also broadens it and increases the rubbery plateau modulus. A translation, the only operation of TTE, cannot capture these changes. Here we establish a time-temperature-composition equivalence (TTCE) from dynamic mechanical measurements of five compositions of a printed family. A shift of the transition along the reduced-frequency axis, a stretch of its breadth and a normalization between its plateaus collapse the storage modulus onto one master curve. The collapse holds at every measured temperature, frequency and composition, through a single reduced variable. The position and breadth of the transition change linearly with the volume fraction of the glassy resin. The phase angle and the relaxation spectrum superpose with the same parameters, so the family shares one distribution of relaxation times. The resulting closed form gives the storage and loss moduli continuously in composition, temperature and frequency, and quantitatively predicts two further mixtures withheld from the calibration. The same shift, stretch and normalization also collapse published temperature sweeps of a patterned composite family of different resins, pointing to broader applicability. Composition thus joins temperature and frequency as a third variable of one equivalence, and the closed form can guide the design of graded and architected printed structures.
item.dc:creator: Beijun Shen, Sanat K. Kumar, Mary C. Boyce

item.title: Compositional neural networks for multimodal X-ray and neutron scattering inversion
item.description: arXiv:2610.29362v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: X-ray and neutron scattering are indispensable for structural characterization across condensed-matter physics and materials science. Yet, because scattering experiments generally record intensities without phase information, distinct structures can yield similar scattering patterns, rendering the corresponding inverse problems non-unique. This ambiguity can be reduced by combining complementary measurements, but their integration into machine-learning frameworks remains challenging. Here we introduce a modular framework for probabilistic multi-measurement analysis based on prior-amortized flow matching. Single-observation posterior estimators are trained separately for individual observation types or physical probes and combined only at inference time through a compositional sampler. This late fusion approach allows pretrained single-observation models to be reused without dedicated joint retraining. As a case in point, we consider reflectometry, which provides depth-resolved, nanometer-scale information about thin films and interfaces. Our single-observation demonstrations span X-ray, time-of-flight neutron and polarized neutron reflectometry. In separate co-refinement studies, task-matched estimators enable homogeneous composition across multiple neutron contrasts and heterogeneous multimodal composition of X-ray and neutron measurements. Together, these results establish compositional flow matching as a modular approach to uncertainty-aware inversion and co-refinement, with potential applicability to other scattering problems in which multiple observations constrain a common physical structure while retaining measurement-specific parameters.
item.dc:creator: Valentin Munteanu, Alexander Hinderhofer, Dmitry Lapkin, Vladimir Starostin, Frank Schreiber

item.title: Momentum-selective graphene spectroscopy of moir\'e excitons
item.description: arXiv:2610.33989v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Far-field photoluminescence probes only the light-cone corner of an exciton's momentum content, whereas energy transfer to nearby graphene integrates in-plane momenta up to the inverse spacer thickness $1/z$. For a WSe$_2$/MoSe$_2$ heterobilayer we build the transition polarization $\bm{P}_n(\qv)$ of each localized moir\'e exciton from the registry-dependent vector dipole texture and use each $\bm{P}_n$ for both baths. The two baths rank the states differently: the graphene-rate ratios differ from the optical ones, their ordering inverts with spacer thickness, and the distance exponents at $z=10$\,nm spread by more than two units. These ratios are independent of the transition-dipole prefactor. Within the $C_3$-symmetric leading-harmonic model the chiral $p_+$ and $d_-$ states are also dark at normal incidence yet transfer to graphene at rates comparable to the bright ground state. Their graphene rate depends on the sign of the texture phase, a quantity invisible in far-field emission, which we determine from first principles. In a device this prediction requires a splitting, larger than the symmetry-breaking mixing, that protects the chiral partners. Graphene proximity thus acts as a momentum-selective near-field probe of moir\'e excitons, and we propose its use as a practical spectroscopy.
